questions.stem: 提示：某高中調查高一與高三學生每週零用錢的用法，下圖是兩個年級平均每週花在飲食、交通、娛樂上的金額，以及存下來的金額。請根據圖表，寫一篇英文作文，文分兩段。第一段描述圖表內容，並比較兩個年級在零用錢用途上最明顯的差異；第二段評估高中生這樣運用零用錢是否恰當，並提出一個能幫助高中生更善用零用錢的具體做法。

高中生的零用錢花在哪裡

1.explanation_zh: 這一題有四個要求：第一段描述圖表、比較兩個年級最明顯的差異；第二段評估這樣用錢是否恰當，並提出幫助高中生善用零用錢的具體做法。圖表的重點有三：兩個年級花最多的都是飲食（450 元、480 元）；高三的娛樂花費只有高一的一半（300 元到 150 元）；高三存下的錢是高一的四倍（100 元到 400 元）。交通幾乎沒變，可以順帶一提。第二段的做法要具體（例如記帳、預算分配），只寫「要多存錢」太空泛。

model_texts.label: steady
model_texts.text:
The chart shows how first-year and third-year students at one high school use their weekly allowance. In both grades, food takes up the largest share of the money. First-year students spend NT$450 a week on food, and third-year students spend NT$480. However, there are two clear differences between the two grades. First, third-year students spend only NT$150 on entertainment, which is half of what first-year students spend. Second, they save NT$400 a week, four times as much as first-year students, who save only NT$100.
In my opinion, third-year students use their allowance more wisely. When I was a first-year student, I often spent my money on snacks and movies, and I had nothing left at the end of the month. As a result, I could not buy a dictionary that I really needed. Saving money is important because it gives us more choices in the future. However, spending a little on fun is not wrong, since it helps us relax. To help students manage their money better, I suggest that students keep a simple spending record on their phones. For example, they can write down what they buy every day and check the total every Sunday night. In this way, they will know where their money goes and save more for the things that really matter.

self_assessment.explanation_zh: 兩段都回應題目：第一段寫出共同點與兩個主要差異，數字正確；第二段有評估、經驗、兼顧娛樂的考量與記帳做法（內容 4）；First、Second 列出差異，段落分工清楚（組織 4）；句子正確，有關係子句與 suggest that 句型，但多為簡單句（文法句構 4）；用字正確但偏基本，spend、money 重複較多（字彙拼字 3）。總分 15，屬穩健版。

model_texts.label: top
model_texts.text:
At first glance, students in the two grades seem to use their allowance in much the same way, since food is the biggest expense for both: first-year students spend NT$450 a week on meals and snacks, while third-year students spend NT$480. A closer look at the other three categories, however, reveals two sharp contrasts. Entertainment, which costs first-year students NT$300 a week, shrinks to just NT$150 for third-year students. That is exactly half the amount. Savings move in the opposite direction, jumping from a modest NT$100 to a substantial NT$400, four times as much. Transportation, by contrast, differs only slightly: NT$150 versus NT$170. In other words, as graduation approaches, students seem to allocate less to games and movies and set aside far more for the future.
I believe this shift reflects growing maturity, and on the whole it is a healthy one. Third-year students know that tuition, rent, and textbooks are waiting for them, so saving becomes a practical goal rather than a vague virtue. I learned this lesson last summer, when I had to borrow NT$3,000 from my parents to join a coding camp because I had wasted most of my allowance on mobile games. Admittedly, cutting entertainment too sharply has its own cost. A weekend movie with friends can relieve the pressure of exam preparation, and teenagers who never spend anything on fun may feel left out. The real problem, then, is not spending itself but spending on impulse, a habit that often begins in the first year. Therefore, I suggest that schools hold a short budgeting workshop for first-year students, in which each student divides a sample allowance into needs, wants, and savings and then tracks real spending with a free app for one month. Students who learn to resist temptation at fifteen will not have to choose between fun and the future; they will simply have planned for both. Managing a few hundred dollars a week may seem trivial, but it is the first rehearsal for managing a whole life.

paragraphs.topic_sentence: At first glance, students in the two grades seem to use their allowance in much the same way, since food is the biggest expense for both: first-year students spend NT$450 a week on meals and snacks, while third-year students spend NT$480.

steady.comment_zh: 四項要求都有回應：第一段點出兩個年級都以飲食花費最多，並用 half of what、four times as much as 讀出娛樂減半與存款四倍兩個主要差異；第二段評估高三較懂得用錢、兼顧適度娛樂，以一年級時買不起字典的經驗佐證，再提出用手機記帳、每週日核對總額的具體做法。缺點是第一段完全沒提交通的金額（規準要四種用途），評估與做法偏簡單；轉承語 However、First、Second、As a result、For example、In this way 清楚但句型變化有限，money、spend 重複偏多。未見文法、用字或標點錯誤。

top.comment_zh: 第一段先寫共同點（飲食最多）再寫兩個鮮明對比（娛樂減半、存款四倍），連交通差距不大也交代，最後歸納為「愈接近畢業愈為未來存錢」；第二段先肯定這是成熟的表現，再以借錢參加營隊的經驗佐證，用 Admittedly 讓步指出娛樂過度縮減的代價，把問題收斂到衝動消費，最後提出高一理財工作坊（需要、想要、儲蓄分配並用 app 追蹤一個月）的具體做法，結尾有見解。句構多變（分詞構句、非限定關係子句、suggest that＋原形、分號），用字精準（allocate、set aside、substantial、on impulse、trivial、rehearsal）。未見錯誤；篇幅偏長、第二段比重大，但不影響分數。

steady.comment_zh: 兩段分工清楚；讀出飲食、娛樂減半、儲蓄四倍等數據與對比，並以買不起字典的經驗和每週記帳提出具體做法。第一段沒寫交通金額（150 與 170 元），圖表描述略不完整；用字平實，spend、money 重複偏多。未發現語言錯誤。

top.comment_zh: 四種用途的金額與兩個明確對比、交通差異小都讀出；第二段先評估再讓步，以借錢參加營隊的經驗帶到預算工作坊的具體做法，結尾有見解。句型多變，用字精準（allocate、impulse、rehearsal），未發現語言錯誤。
